newsitem.title: USA: U.S. refiners urge delay on air standards changes.
newsitem.headline: U.S. refiners urge delay on air standards changes.

text.p: The National Petroleum Refiners Association in statements prepared for public hearings this week urged the Clinton administration to postpone strengthening air quality standards.

NPRA representatives, slated to attended public hearings being held Tuesday and Wednesday in three cities across the country, said the administration's plan would impose higher costs on U.S. refiners that would put them at a disadvantage to overseas refiners.

The NPRA also said "overly stringent" air quality standards "threaten the viability of the domestic refining industry and its ability to meet future energy needs of U.S. consumers for gasoline, diesel fuel, home heating oil, and other products."
The Environmental Protection Agency in late November proposed setting more stringent standards against smog and soot air pollution, saying existing standards did not adequately protect public health.
For the first time, the EPA proposed setting a special standard for tiny air particles produced from car exhaust and industrial combustion.
The NPRA, along with a number of other industry groups, contended that the air is getting cleaner, and that health benefits from complying with current standards have not fully been evaluated.
It said the EPA particularly lacked information on tiny particles, which it has not monitored comprehensively.
The NPRA also said the EPA should evaluate potential costs of changing the standards now, not later when it is developing plans on how to meet the new standards.

"Our worst fear is that a new fine particulate standard will be implemented, additional draconian measures will be imposed on society, and in the end, the real cause of these health concerns will remain unaddressed," the NPRA said.
